messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David, a 54-year-old civil servant, presented as a man stretched taut, his affable demeanour a thin veneer over a constant, humming anxiety. He had been with his new partner, Tom, for a year, but the stability of the relationship had only served to highlight the disarray within his own mind. The trauma occurred two years prior, at the hands of his then-partner, Mark. The abuse had been escalating for months, but it culminated in a single night of terrifying violence where David was physically overpowered and held down, an experience of absolute helplessness that became the new anchor for his sense of self in the world.

The memories of that night do not arrive as a coherent story. When David tries to deliberately recall the sequence of events, he finds the memory frustratingly inaccessible, a locked room in his mind. Yet, it intrudes upon him without warning, not as a film, but as a series of stark, high-definition photographs. He will see a still image of the bedroom wallpaper, a flash of Mark’s face, the overturned bedside lamp. These photographic intrusions are often accompanied by a visceral sensory echo: the coppery taste of blood in his mouth, sharp and sudden, which can send him reeling in the middle of a workday. These fragmented memories make the world feel unpredictable and dangerous, and because they are so disconnected from a narrative, he feels haunted by them, certain they mean he is permanently broken.

This profound sense of impending threat has reshaped his daily existence, particularly in his work environment. Being alone with another man, a routine part of his job in a large government agency, has become an ordeal. A recent one-on-one meeting with his line manager triggered a cascade of symptoms. The quiet closing of the office door felt like a trap, a loss of control that was sickeningly familiar. This feeling immediately brought forth the photographic stills of the assault, the taste of blood filling his mouth as he tried to focus on quarterly reports. In response to such triggers, David has developed a set of rigid, exhausting rules for living. He now insists on having a third person present in meetings with male colleagues, an accommodation his department has found increasingly puzzling. After work, he orchestrates a frantic schedule of social events, ensuring he is never alone with his thoughts. He has become the life of the party out of sheer terror, keeping himself surrounded by people until he can fall into bed, exhausted, next to Tom.

This relentless avoidance has, in turn, amplified his fears. By constantly surrounding himself with people, he has taught his nervous system that solitude is the ultimate danger. The rare moments he is forced to be alone—like when Tom went on a business trip last month—are now sources of profound panic. The prospect of sleeping by himself in their quiet apartment was so terrifying that it brought on another night of intrusive photographic memories. The experience cemented his belief that he cannot cope on his own, making him even more desperate to avoid it in the future. His strategy of mentally detaching from the memories, of treating them like a story about someone else, has also backfired. This detachment prevents any kind of processing, so when the memories do break through, they feel alien and overwhelmingly powerful, reinforcing his sense of being out of control and at their mercy.

The self-reinforcing cycle has tightened its grip over the past year. A trigger, like the prospect of sleeping alone, unleashes the fragmented, sensory-rich memories. The horror of these memories makes the trigger seem even more life-threatening. This heightened sense of threat then fuels his desperate attempts to avoid being alone or to mentally push the memories away. But this very avoidance is what preserves the memories’ toxic power and makes the triggers more potent the next time they arise. The life he has built to protect himself has become his prison. It was after Tom gently confronted him, expressing deep concern about his inability to ever be alone or to talk about his past, that David finally sought help. He came to therapy not with a clear goal, but with a simple, desperate question: "How do I learn to be in a room by myself again?"
